Canada Faces Scrutiny Over Environmental Policy Incoherence Ahead of COP17 Biodiversity Summit

28 Oct 2026, 08:49 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily Climate Desk · Source: www.cbc.ca

As Environment and Climate Change Minister Julie Dabrusin departs for the United Nations COP17 biodiversity conference in Yerevan, Armenia, Canada's international conservation pledges are being weighed against domestic legislative changes that critics argue could fast-track industrial development at the expense of ecological protection.

Dabrusin travels to the summit aiming to position Canada for a leadership role in global nature preservation and emission reduction. The international gathering follows a series of high-profile domestic conservation announcements by Ottawa.

Recent Conservation Pledges and Global Commitments

In October, the federal government announced the protection of a forest and peatland area near Kapuskasing, Ontario, measuring 1.3 times the size of Toronto. Additionally, Ottawa has backed the Northwest Territories' 'Our Land for the Future' initiative, a massive Indigenous-led conservation project covering 380,000 square kilometres of land and water, roughly equivalent to the size of Japan.

These moves align with Canada's participation in the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, co-hosted by Canada and China, which established a global target to protect 30 per cent of the world's lands and waters by 2030. However, UN Secretary General António Guterres recently noted that global progress toward these targets remains slow, warning that current commitments fall short of the 2030 goals.

Domestic Criticism and Legislative Contradictions

Dabrusin's presence in Armenia coincides with mounting domestic backlash over Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act. Currently moving through the House of Commons, the omnibus bill proposes amendments to several environmental laws to expedite federal jurisdiction over pipelines, power lines, and mines.

Environmental advocates, including Greenpeace Canada campaigner Salomé Sané, have labeled the government's approach as policy incoherence, questioning how Ottawa can advocate for conservation abroad while advancing legislation that critics claim bypasses key environmental regulations.

In response to the criticism, Dabrusin defended the government's stance, noting that some initial legislative amendments were dropped following pushback. She maintained that BillC-39 focuses on streamlining project assessments rather than lowering environmental safeguards.

Practical Implications and Reader Verification

For readers monitoring Canadian environmental policy and international commitments, the situation highlights the complex balancing act between resource development and conservation goals.

  • What is confirmed: Minister Julie Dabrusin is attending the UN COP17 biodiversity summit in Armenia. Canada has recently announced significant domestic conservation areas in Ontario and the Northwest Territories. Bill C-39 is currently before the House of Commons to amend environmental legislation for major projects.
  • What remains unknown: The final text and exact implementation impacts of Bill C-39 are still subject to parliamentary debate and potential amendments. The long-term success of global 2030 biodiversity targets remains under scrutiny by UN officials.
  • How to verify: Readers can review official federal announcements and track legislative progress through the Parliament of Canada website or read the original reporting via the [CBC News report](https://www.cbc.ca/news/politics/cop17-united-nations-biodiversity-conference-armenia-9.7393740).
